When a node disconnects and quickly reconnects with {{port_range=0}} (fixed port – as we use in WildFly for all sockets), the OS may keep the old server socket in TIME_WAIT for up to 60-120 seconds. Without SO_REUSEADDR, the {{bind()}} call in {{Util.createServerSocket}} and {{Util.createServerSocketChannel}} fails with {{BindException}} because the OS considers the address still in use. With {{port_range=0}} there is no fallback port, so the node cannot rejoin – so this won’t normally happen with JGroups configuration in the project.

Fix is to set SO_REUSEADDRESS on these sockets.

BaseServer.send() can leave a dangling connection when stop() runs concurrently:

# send() passes validateArgs() (running is still true)
# stop() sets running=false and clears conns
# send() calls getConnection() which creates a _new_ connection and adds it to conns
# send completes without exception — the connection is never cleaned up

The connection remains in the conns map but the server is stopped. This can cause a departed member to persist in the coordinator's view, resulting in a duplicate node upon reconnection.

BaseServer.send() can leave a dangling connection when stop() runs concurrently:

# send() passes validateArgs() (running is still true)
# stop() sets running=false and clears conns
# send() calls getConnection() which creates a _new_ connection and adds it to conns
# send completes without exception — the connection is never cleaned up

The connection remains in the conns map but the server is stopped. This can cause a departed member to persist in the coordinator's view, resulting in a duplicate node upon reconnection ("double node" problem from JGRP-2974).

The original PR #984 proposed a finally block in both send() overloads to remove the connection if the server is no longer running. This part of the fix was not included when the graceful close mechanism (JGRP-2974) was implemented.

Fix: add a finally block to both send(Address, byte[], int, int) and send(Address, ByteBuffer) that checks !running() and calls removeConnectionIfPresent(). This is safe because removeConnectionIfPresent is idempotent (CAS on ConcurrentHashMap).

Util.createServerSocketChannel(SocketFactory, String, InetAddress, int start_port, int end_port, int) probes ports in [start_port .. end_port]. On each iteration it creates a ServerSocketChannel via the SocketFactory (which allocates a file descriptor) and then attempts to bind().

When bind() throws a SocketException (e.g. "Address already in use") on a terminal path, the just-created channel is not closed before the method throws, leaking its file descriptor (only reclaimed on GC).

Since JGRP-2426 (commit fdf059e5c, Jan 2020) removed all stats collection from JChannel and moved it to MsgStats in the transport protocol, the {{stats}} field and its accessors ({{getStats()}}, {{stats()}}, {{setStats()}}, {{stats(boolean)}}) on JChannel are dead code — the field can be set but nothing reads it.

WildFly currently calls {{channel.stats(configuration.isStatisticsEnabled())}} which sets this boolean to no effect. The actual statistics collection is controlled by {{Protocol.enableStats()}}.

These should be deprecated (and eventually removed) to avoid confusion.

With some of the more recent JDKs, sending of byte arrays and receiving of data is done via *direct* {{ByteBuffers}}. 

When sending a byte[] array, a temporary direct {{ByteBuffer }}is fetched from a cache, the array is copied into the{{ByteBuffer }}and the latter is then passed to{{ NioSocketImpl.implWrite(). }}If a buffer with the required length is not found, a new one will be created (slow operation) and added to the cache.

Apparently, a write from a direct ByteBuffer is more efficient when the buffer is passed from Java to kernel space.

When receiving a message, a temporary direct ByteBuffer is created and passed to the socket’s receive operation. The contents are then copied to the byte[] array passed as argument.

Goal:

* Make bundler implementations (BaseBundler) provide a direct ByteBuffer instead of a byte[] array, which is then passed to the transport. This avoids having to maintain a cache of direct ByteBuffers
* Make the receivers (UDP.PacketReceiver, TcpConnection, NioConnection) use direct ByteBuffers for reception of messages
* Whether byte arrays or (direct) ByteBuffers are used should be configurable (in the bundler). There should be a sanity check to see if there’s a mismatch between a bundler buffer matches the type of the transport. Example: if the bundler uses a byte array as buffer, but the transport is {{TCP_NIO2}} (with direct memory) → issue a warning

Changes:

* All transports (UDP, TCP, TCP_NIO2) need to implement doSend(ByteBuffer) in addition to doSend(byte[])
* Make sure to collect multiple smaller writes in the serialization in a heap-buffer and only write to the direct buffer once, as this is supposedly faster (verify with JMH)
* Make {{ByteBufferOutputStream}} expandable, similar to {{ByteArrayDataOutputStream}}

On my box, a send takes 3.5us. Measure if there is any performance increase when using direct byte buffers.

Apparently, a write from a direct ByteBuffer is more efficient when the buffer is passed from Java to kernel space.

When receiving a message, a temporary direct ByteBuffer is created and passed to the socket’s receive operation. The contents are then copied to the byte[] array passed as argument.

Goal:

* Make bundler implementations (BaseBundler) provide a direct ByteBuffer instead of a byte[] array, which is then passed to the transport. This avoids having to maintain a cache of direct ByteBuffers
* Make the receivers (UDP.PacketReceiver, TcpConnection, NioConnection) use direct ByteBuffers for reception of messages
* Whether byte arrays or (direct) ByteBuffers are used should be configurable (in the bundler). There should be a sanity check to see if there’s a mismatch between a bundler buffer matches the type of the transport. Example: if the bundler uses a byte array as buffer, but the transport is {{TCP_NIO2}} (with direct memory) → issue a warning

Changes:

* All transports (UDP, TCP, TCP_NIO2) need to implement doSend(ByteBuffer) in addition to doSend(byte[])
* Make sure to collect multiple smaller writes in the serialization in a heap-buffer and only write to the direct buffer once, as this is supposedly faster (verify with JMH)

On my box, a send takes 3.5us. Measure if there is any performance increase when using direct byte buffers.

items.toString:
The problem with the current open/accept logic in multiple jvm is that it might cause the system to lead to a singleton cluster member when 2 or more nodes tries to interconnect with each other.
This happens when usually when VERIFY_SUSPECTS and DISCOVERY protocols collide at the same time causing connection rejections. The problem can be dicompose in others.

1. ack/nack connections. When  we tried to open a connection and get a connection during handling incoming connection it might happen that the connection being created is rejected therefore useless for any GSM/Discovery response causing the channel to think that is isolated.
2. handle accept reject algorithm based on port don't work under certain conditions when two jvm try to compete. It is require to get some exchange information based on shared knowledge instead of basing the algorithm in the ports providing by the operating system that we don't have any control how they are going to be provided.
3. handling incoming / outgoing connections should be lock based on the destination. It is possible to find in the "enableSuspects" this case where the discovery protocol / merge leads to opening a connection and verify suspects leads to open a connections having at least 2 jvm trying to open and accepting a connection from the same for the same peer_address in different jvm. e.g:

1. jvm A open a connection to jvm B (B outgoing in A)
2. jvm B open a connection to jvm A (A address outgoing in B)
3. jvm B accepts connection from jvm A (A ddress incoming in B)
4. jvm A accepts a connection from jvm B (B incoming in A)

This scenarios could lead to the points above:
E.g:
Scenario where A opens a connection to B
B opens a connection to A
A beats B therefore B handle accept rejects the connection so A handling connections have a closed connection and the operation being performed fails. (scenario 1)

Another scenario is where the ports satisfy both things at the same time as you opened connections but and ports fulfil the port rejection algorithm as the port is higher already (it is not bullet proof)

The last scenario vis that opening a connection and handling a connection need to somehow being sync as they belong to the same scenario (they are producing a connection to an endpoint)

h4. Summary

In a cluster, {{NAKACK4}} using {{FixedBuffer}} can end up with a permanently full send/receive window and block the sender after a finite number of multicast messages. This happens when {{{}xmit_from_random_member=true{}}}, because it effectively disables discarding of delivered messages ({{{}discard_delivered_msgs=false{}}}), preventing the receive windows from being purged and the sender from making forward progress.

{{*Setup protocol stack*}}

 
{code:java}
Protocol[] protStack = {
          new TCP()
              .setBindPort(bindPort)
              .setBindAddress(bindAddress)
              .setExternalAddr(externalAddress)
              .setValue("enable_suspect_events", true),

          new TCPPING()
              .setPortRange(0)
              .initialHosts(initialHosts),

          new MERGE3(),

          new FD_ALL3(),

          new VERIFY_SUSPECT2(),

          new NAKACK4()
              .capacity(100)
              .setXmitFromRandomMember(true),

          new GMS(),

          new FRAG3()
      };{code}
*Steps to reproduce:*
 # Start cluster with two members (A and B)
 # A tries to multicast 400 messages

*Observed behavior:*
 * B blocks after 100 messages
 * A blocks indefinitely after 200 messages because it did not receive ACKs for last 100 messages and the send window is full
 * Receive windows ({{{}xmit_table {}}}entries) are not purged because delivered messages are retained when {{discard_delivered_msgs=false}}
 * Adding {{STABLE}} to the stack does not resolve the issue (NAKACK4 does not rely on STABLE to purge state)
 * Same happens for clusters with 3 members

*Expected behavior:*

Even when {{xmit_from_random_member=true, {{NAKACK4}}}} should eventually be able to *reclaim buffer space* once all members have *delivered/ACKed* the messages.

Provide new annotations or changes to annotation attributes to enable jgroups-opentelemetry to generate OTEL code directly from JGroups protocols.

Currently, jgroups-opentelemetry creates a parallel hierarchy to JGroups protocols and registers attributes programmatically.

We need to come up with and agree on a common translation between JGroups annotations (e.g. {{AttributeType.SCALAR}} -> {{Counter}}) and provide new annotations or annotation attributes in JGroups to accommodate jgroups-opentelemetry (e.g. {{Gauge}}?).

h3. Observable

|| jgroups-otel || JGroups ||
| Observable | ManagedAttribute, Property |
| Observable.name | name |
| Observable.type -> ObservableType | type -> AttributeType |
| Observable.unit -> ObservableUnit | unit -> TimeUnit |
| Observable.description | description |


h3. ObservableType

|| jgroups-otel || JGroups || Comments ||
| ObservableType.COUNTER | AttributeType.SCALAR | We can probably use UP_DOWN_COUNTER everywhere |
| ObservableType.UP_DOWN_COUNTER | AttributeType.SCALAR | |
| ObservableType.GAUGE | gauge=true| |
| ObservableType.HISTOGRAM | not used | |

h3. ObservableUnit

| ObservableUnit.UNITY | unit missing |
| ObservableUnit.NANOSECONDS | unit.NANOSECONDS |
| ObservableUnit.MILLISECONDS | unit.MILLISECONDS |
| ObservableUnit.SECONDS | unit.SECONDS |
| ObservableUnit.BYTES | type.BYTES |
| ObservableUnit.KILOBYTES | type.BYTES (compute kB) |
| ObservableUnit.MEGABYTES | type.BYTES (compute MB) |


h3. ObservableScope
| ObservableScope.RUNTIME | ManagedAttribute  |
| ObservableScope.CONFIGURATION | Property |


Make sure that fields annotated with Property and {{exposedAsManagedAttribute=false}} are *not* shown, as they might contain sensistive information, such as passwords etc.

h3. Transformations

* Only {{ManagedAtributes}} are metrics, the {{Property}} annotation is configuration (not mapped?)
* All {{SCALAR}} / {{TIME}} / {{BYTES}} types -> {{COUNTER}}
** Example: bytes sent/received
** Can this be reset to 0?
* Add {{ManagedAttribute.gauge}} attribute to JGroups. Values that have no correlation to previous values, e.g. number of threads, average state size, total number of bytes in send-queue
** Maps to {{GAUGE}} (or {{UP_DOWN_COUNTER}}?)
* How do we map {{Average/AverageMinMax}}? {{HISTOGRAM}} ?
* Bytes are mapped to KB, MB etc. This can be computed dynamically
* Time is always milliseconds unless `unit` is present

Examples:

|| JGroups attribute || jgroups-otel || Description ||
| UDP.msg_stats.num_ucasts_sent (LongAdder), SCALAR | COUNTER | |
| UDP.msg_stats.num_mcast_bytes_sent (LongAdder), BYTES | COUNTER | |
| UFC.avg_time_blocked (double), TIME gauge=true | GAUGE | |
| UNICAST3.xmit_table_undelivered_messages (long), gauge=true | GAUGE | |



[1] https://github.com/rhusar/jgroups-opentelemetry

Provide new annotations or changes to annotation attributes to enable jgroups-opentelemetry to generate OTEL code directly from JGroups protocols.

Currently, jgroups-opentelemetry creates a parallel hierarchy to JGroups protocols and registers attributes programmatically.

We need to come up with and agree on a common translation between JGroups annotations (e.g. {{AttributeType.SCALAR}} -> {{Counter}}) and provide new annotations or annotation attributes in JGroups to accommodate jgroups-opentelemetry (e.g. {{Gauge}}?).

items.fromString:
* There is an incorrect calculation of timeout. System.nano is not a clock and it is getting mixed System.currentTimeMillis. System.nanonTime has a different origin of time than System.currentTimeMillis. This comparison results in timing out suspect that has not beeing expired.
* The timeout thread is not stopped during disconnect (only shutdown). If we are working in memory it can create phantom suspect events as it might run from disconnect operation and sending the suspect all the way up if the suspect_events is active. The thread is still going even when the stop operation happens.
* locking problems: within thread execution is locking on This instead of VERIFY_SUSPECT2.this which is the lock for suspects and runtime this can cause concurrent access problem to the Set (as it is not sync)

The {{BasicTCP.enableSuspectEvents}} feature currently lacks comprehensive test coverage, particularly for scenarios involving graceful node departures from the cluster. This test gap has allowed critical issues to exist undetected and uncovered in WildFly.

  Test Reproducer:
  A new test {{EnableSuspectEventsTest.testRepeatedLeaveAndJoin()}} has been created to reproduce this scenario. The test:

  - Creates a 3-node cluster using TCP transport with {{enableSuspectEvents(true)}}
  - Repeatedly makes the coordinator leave gracefully
  - Verifies that remaining nodes stay together in a single cluster (not forming singleton clusters)
  - Uses {{TCPPING}} with {{numDiscoveryRuns(3)}} to reliably trigger the race condition
  - Runs for 500 iterations to ensure stability

  Configuration Details:
  The test mimics a typical WildFly cluster configuration with:
  - {{TCP}} protocol with {{enableSuspectEvents(true)}}
  - {{TCPPING}} discovery with {{numDiscoveryRuns(3)}} (critical for reproducing the bug not sure why)
  - Standard WildFly protocol stack ({{NAKACK4}}, {{UNICAST4}}, {{GMS}}, etc.)

  Expected Behavior:
  When the coordinator leaves gracefully:
  - Remaining nodes should receive and process the {{LEAVE_REQ}}
  - Remaining nodes should install a new view with size {{N-1}}
  - All remaining nodes should stay in the same cluster (no singleton clusters)
  - Connection closures should NOT trigger spurious {{SUSPECT}} events that cause cluster splits

Currently, {{org.jgroups.tests.Probe}} class does all the heavy lifting and has all the infrastructure needed to contact a cluster to retrieve metrics/status/perform managed operations. This opens the possibility of utilizing {{Probe}} as a client API to develop custom scripts that require access to the cluster nodes.

One existing limitation is that {{Probe}} automatically redirects the response to the standard output. To have more flexibility using it to develop the client side, we need an API to register a custom response handler, so instead of writing to standard output, the response is passed to the user's handler.

Ideally, this custom handler should receive the {{Address}} of which node sent the response, and the `{{ByteArray}}` payload, with the actual response. If the custom handler is installed, nothing is written to standard output.

I did the following test locally with our {{JdbcPing2Test}} that does 100 iterations.

Before the change: 63x "no physical address, 8:53 runtime

After the change: 36x "no physical address", 6:13 runtime

Keycloak issue: [https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43357]

Provide new (default: no-op) methods in {{Message}}:
* {{incr()}}: increments the reference count
* {{decr()}}: decrements the reference count
* {{refCount()}}: gets the reference count

Method {{incr()}} is called when a message is sent, {{decr()}} when (1) {{NAKACK}} or {{UNICAST}} release the message (removal from the retransmission table) and (2) when the send returns.

When the reference count goes from 1 to 0, the resource associated with the message (e.g. a pooled bytebuf) can be released.

items.fromString:
Non-blocking flow control is somewhat of a misnomer: {{UFC_NB}} and {{MFC_NB}} do block, but just later; instead of blocking immediately, they queue requests and (because the queue is bounded) block on a full queue later.

This might cover a temporary peak, but if producers are faster than consumers, producers will eventually need to block. Even for temporary peaks, it might be better to block producers immediately rather than delaying the blocking.

In addition, with the addition of {{UNICAST4}} and {{NAKACK4}}, blocking is done directly in these protocols rather than in the flow control protocols, so having just 1 set ({{UFC}} and {{MFC}}) should be enough.

I'll therefore remove {{UFC_NB}} and {{MFC_NB}}.
